newsitem.title: USA: CBOT wheat sets fresh 7-month high on freeze fears.
newsitem.headline: CBOT wheat sets fresh 7-month high on freeze fears.

text.p: Severe damage expected from a weekend freeze in portions of the U.S. Great Plains hard red winter belt boosted CBOT soft red winter wheat futures to limit gains as well as a fresh seven-month high in the nearby May contract, traders said.
"It looks like there was a lot of damage and there's a chance of frost again tonight plus there are problems in Europe," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.
Kansas State University wheat breeder, Rollie Sears said "we had a good crop and basically the potential for a good crop is out the window. Right now it is pretty depressing."

May set a session high of $4.23 a bushel, the highest for that contract since $4.23-1/2 was notched September 11. A nine-month high was set in active new crop July of $4.28-1/4, the highest level since $4.29 was reached on July 15. September settled limit up and at its new contract high of $4.32.

A buying pool of roughly 14 million bushels was noted at the close, with 10 million wanted in the July. Action in options indicated Tuesday's open for the July would be at $4.36 to $4.38 per bushel, up eight to 10 cents.
Wheat closed 10-1/2 to 20 cents per bushel higher, with May up 20 at $4.23.
Wheat futures on Tuesday will trade with expanded 30-cent-per-bushel trading limits.

The weekend freeze caused little if any damage to U.S. soft red winter wheat, agronomists and grain dealers said. But concern persisted about possible late seedings of U.S. spring wheat because of wet, cold weather and flooding in some areas.

But harm definitely occurred over the weekend in the HRW wheat region, with damage likely in areas spanning Kansas through Oklahoma into Texas, the heart of the HRW producing area, sources in those areas said.

Travis Miller, agronomist at Texas A&M University said the HRW crop in Texas was likely to suffer major losses. Curtis Thompson, Kansas State University extension agronomist said it will take a "miracle" for wheat in his region, which includes 24 counties in southwest Kansas, to survive. Al Peterlin, chief meteorologist with the U.S. Agriculture Department said "there's no question we have done some damage and caused some stress to the (HRW wheat) plants."
"We've heard anywhere from 95 million to 250 million bushels were lost," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter.
But the U.S. crop wasn't the only area of concern during Monday's frantic limit-up move in CBOT wheat.

The French farm ministry added its own voice Monday to early predictions of drought there with a tentative warning that winter cereals and rapeseed crops could be damaged if there is no break in the weather soon.
Also, forecasters said the dry weather, which has forced prices up in European grains markets, will likely continue this week.
In addition, Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE) wheat futures moved up sharply in heavy trading Monday as Australian dry weather worsened and on world supply concerns.
Wheat futures volume was estimated by the CBOT at 15,000 contracts, below the 41,039 traded Friday.

In wheat options, FIMAT Futures bought 1,800 July $3.90 puts and sold 1,800 July $4.10 puts and was a featured buyer of the July $4.30 calls, traders said. Fimat was a key bear spreader of four million bushels of July/May at five cents, premium July, traders said.
Wheat options volume was estimated at 30,000 contracts, below the record volume of 35,240 traded on April 30, 1996 but above the 27,914 traded Friday.
